opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that a seed round, even a large one, doesn't change what kind of company we are. We're still a research lab at heart. The funding buys time and compute, and that matters, but the real question is whether we can use that time to do something that the big labs aren't already doing better.

That's how I think about our position. We're not trying to beat the frontier labs at their own game. Scaling up language models is a race with a very clear scoreboard, and you need enormous resources to stay in it. Our bet is different. We believe that if you want intelligence that actually understands the physical world, that can plan and reason about consequences, language alone isn't enough. You need world models, systems that learn from video, from interaction, from sensory data, and build an internal representation of how the world works. That's a long-term research direction, and honestly it's the kind of thing a startup can be more focused on than a large company with many product pressures.

So in a way, being small is an advantage. We can commit to a thesis. We don't have to ship a chatbot next quarter. But it's also a responsibility. Investors gave us room to explore, and we need to show real research progress, not just talk about a vision. In the early stage, I think our job is to attract the right people, people who are excited by hard, open problems rather than incremental benchmarks, and to build a culture that's open, that publishes, that stays connected to the academic community.

I'd also say there's some humility needed. Many people have tried to build world models. The idea isn't new. What's new is that the tools, the data, and the compute are finally at a point where it might work. Whether we're the ones who get there, nobody knows. But I think it's worth trying, and I'd rather be in a place where we can try it seriously than watch from the side.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes making use of the funding for research and showing research progress, but it does not clearly say that achieving a research breakthrough matters more than securing the seed funding.

r002.rationale: The response acknowledges that many have tried to build world models and that success is uncertain, but it does not say that others’ disbelief motivates Xie.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll be honest, I think the word "startup" slightly undersells what AMI Labs is trying to do, and at the same time it's exactly the right word for how we have to operate.

Let me explain both halves. On the ambition side, this isn't a company built around one product or one model release. The whole premise is that the current paradigm, scaling autoregressive language models on text, is not going to get us to systems that actually understand the physical world, that can plan, that have persistent memory, that reason about consequences before acting. Yann has been saying this for years, and I've come to the same place from the vision side. So the research agenda is world models, self-supervised learning from video and sensory data, architectures like JEPA that learn in representation space instead of predicting every pixel or every token. That's a long-horizon bet. You don't do that in eighteen months.

On the other side, a seed round means we are small, and that's a real constraint, but I actually see it as an advantage right now. The big labs are enormously well resourced, but they're also locked in. Their revenue, their infrastructure, their hiring, their public commitments are all organized around the current paradigm. It's very hard to turn a ship that size. A small lab with a clear thesis can make choices that would be organizationally impossible inside a big company. We don't have to ship a chatbot. We don't have to defend a leaderboard every quarter.

So the position I'd describe is something like a focused research institution with startup discipline. The seed money buys us time and compute to prove the core ideas, and the real test isn't whether we raise the next round. It's whether, in a couple of years, the world-model approach shows capabilities that the token-prediction approach fundamentally can't. If it does, the resources follow. If it doesn't, we'll have learned something important either way.

What I'd say to people watching from outside is: don't evaluate us the way you'd evaluate a company racing to catch up to the frontier labs on their own benchmarks. We're explicitly not playing that game. Evaluate us on whether we open a different door. That's a riskier position, honestly, but I think it's the only interesting one to be in right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the real test is whether the world-model approach demonstrates new capabilities, not whether AMI raises another round; this makes the research breakthrough the priority over securing funding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the seed round gives us room to explore, but it’s still the beginning. Funding doesn’t mean we’ve solved the hard problems or proved that our approach will work. It gives us the opportunity to build a strong team, test our ideas, and learn quickly.

For me, the interesting question is how we turn that opportunity into real progress. As a startup, we need to be ambitious about the research while staying disciplined about what we can actually demonstrate. That’s how I’d view our position: we have a chance to build something meaningful, and now we have to earn it.

r001.rationale: The response says funding enables exploration and stresses research progress, but it does not say achieving a research breakthrough matters more than securing the seed funding.
